1005.t: Possibly from the stem *kʷern̥t- of Proto-Indo-European *kwéronts, active participle of *kʷéreti (“to do, make, perform (magic, etc.)”), thematic variant of *kʷért, in any case from the root *kʷer-, or formed within Greek from a lost verb *τέρω (*térō) +…

1072.t: A proper noun use of the substantivized adjective χριστός (khrīstós, “anointed; consecrated”), employed as the Greek equivalent of semantic loan from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (mašīaḥ) and Aramaic ܡܫܺܝܚܳܐ (m'šīḥāʿ).

1003.t: From πορνεύω (porneúō, “to prostitute, to whore”) + -ία (-íā, “-ia: forming abstract nouns”), from πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute, whore”) + -εύω (-eúō, forming verbs), from the Proto-Indo-European root *perh₂- (“to sell, to provide for a fee”).

1010.t: From Proto-Hellenic *húpnos, from Proto-Indo-European *supnós (“sleep”). Cognate with Sanskrit स्वप्न (svápna) and Albanian gjumë < *źúpnos.

1012.t: Of Northwest Semitic origin. See Hebrew דַּמֶּשֶׂק (dammeśeq).

1038.t: Unknown; often compared with the second element of Middle Irish gairb-driuch (“bristle”) and Lithuanian drikà (“threads hanging from the loom”), though Beekes rejects both connections and leaves the origin unknown, noting that the semantic roots used to…

1061.t: From παραβάλλω (parabállō, “to set side by side”) + -η (-ē).

1034.t: Possibly inherited from Proto-Indo-European *gláktn̥ (“milk”) (compare Latin lact, Old Armenian կաթն (katʻn), Albanian dhallë), earlier *glákt (or, if the Hittite cognate is valid, *gláktr̥), perhaps from a root *glag- + *-tr̥, but the phonetic…

1046.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰórtos (“enclosure”). Cognates include Sanskrit गृह (gṛhá), Latin hortus, and Old English ġeard (English yard).

1053.t: Borrowed from Old Persian 𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎢𐏁 (d-a-r-y-u-š /⁠Dārayauš⁠/), shortened form of 𐎭𐎠𐎼𐎹𐎺𐎢𐏁 (d-a-r-y-v-u-š /⁠Dārayavaʰuš⁠/).

1052.t: From Proto-Hellenic *oktṓ, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Cognates include Sanskrit अष्ट (aṣṭa), Latin octō, and Old English eahta (English eight).

1083.t: From ἀ- (a-) + βυθός (buthós, “depth of the sea”) Compare Sanskrit अगाध (agādha, “fathomless; abyss, chasm”).

1089.t: Borrowed from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew”), likely through Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”).

1060.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to wed”), and compared with Latin nūbō (“to marry”) (whence English nubile).

1008.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *woǵʰlos, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to drive, transport”) (whence also ὄχος (ókhos) and Arcadocypriot Greek ϝέχω (wékhō, “to bear, bring”)), with cognates such as Old Norse vagl.

1031.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷarus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us. Cognate to Sanskrit गुरु (gurú), Latin gravis.

1032.t: From βραχύς (brăkhŭ́s, “short”) + -ίων (-ī́ōn, comparative suffix), literally “the shorter one”, because the upper arm is shorter than the forearm.

1064.t: Uncertain. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *stl̥-n-eh₂, from *stel- (“to put, place”) (related to στέλλω (stéllō, “to set, arrange”)), with similarities to Old High German stollo.

1014.t: From Proto-Hellenic *déspotis, an original phrase from Proto-Indo-European *déms pótis (“master of the house”), from *dṓm (“house”), whence also Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos, “house”); and *pótis (“master”), whence also Ancient Greek πόσις (pósĭs,…

1021.t: From Proto-Indo-European *teh₂- (“to melt”). Cognates include Latin tābeō, Sanskrit तोयम् (toyam), Old Armenian թանամ (tʻanam, “to wet”) and Old English þawian (English thaw), Proto-Slavic *tajati (Russian та́ять (tájatʹ)).

1011.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₃émōs. Cognates include Sanskrit अंस॑ (áṃsa), Latin umerus, Old Armenian ուս (us), and Gothic 𐌰𐌼𐍃 (ams).

1076.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pikrós, formally identical to Proto-Slavic *pьstrъ (“variegated”), which is from Proto-Indo-European *piḱ-rós, from the root *peyḱ- (“color, speckle”).

1042.t: From Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash; to bathe”). Cognates include Albanian laj, Latin lavō, Old Armenian լոգանամ (loganam), and Old English lēaþor (English lather).

1096.t: Borrowed from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā), from Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ).

1033.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷōmós, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷoh₂mós, from *gʷeh₂- (“to step”) (whence ἔβην (ébēn)). Compare βῆμα (bêmă, “step”).

1004.t: From Proto-Indo-European *kʷendʰ-; cognate with πάθος (páthos) and πάσχω (páskhō).

1077.t: Usually derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷes- (“to extinguish, quell”).

1073.t: From θαυμάζω (thaumázō, “to admire, be surprised at”) + -τός (-tós, adjective suffix).

1027.t: Ordinal of ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”). The term derives from earlier *ὄγδοϝος (*ógdowos), itself perhaps from earlier Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓwos, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.

1097.t: Has been connected with Old Norse þefja (“to stamp”) and þóf (“crowd”) but this theory is not convincing. Probably from Pre-Greek.

1078.t: The traditional Indo-European analysis reconstructed *strebʰ- (“to twist”) and compared it with Proto-West Germanic *stroppōn (“to twist, writhe”).

1043.t: From μάλα (mắlă, “very”) + *-ϳον (*-jon, comparative suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“strong, big”), with long α (a) perhaps after ἆσσον (âsson). Cognates include Latin melior (“better”).

1007.t: From the root of ἱκνέομαι (hiknéomai, “to be appropriate”) + -νος (-nos).

1026.t: Probably from ἐν (en, “in; at”) + Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“hand; to curve”, whence γυῖον (guîon, “hand”)), ἐγγύη (engŭ́ē, “pledge; security”)), thus literally, “at hand”.

1047.t: From ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).

1016.t: The word is presumably the negative prefix νη- (nē-), but the stem is unclear.

1062.t: Traditionally derived from πορφύρω (porphúrō, “(of waves) to heave, boil, surge up”), itself related to φύρω (phúrō, “to mix”), Hittite 𒁍𒊒𒌓 (purut, “mud, soil”) and Sanskrit भुरति (bhuráti, “have convulsions, sprawl”).

1025.t: From Proto-Indo-European *welh₃- (“to catch, seize, strike”) + -σκομαι (-skomai). The aspiration was probably taken from αἱρεῖν (haireîn) and/or ἑλεῖν (heleîn).

1087.t: From earlier *ἐπι-hίσταμαι (*epi-hístamai), with early loss of the breath *-h- and vowel contraction, with sense development "stand before something" > "be confronted with something" > "take knowledge of something" similar to that of Proto-West Germanic…

1015.t: From Proto-Indo-European *leyb-, the same root as λείβω (leíbō, “to pour”).

1098.t: Derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-. Doublet of χέω (khéō, “to pour”).

1051.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂eHs- Proto-Indo-European *-tḗr Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hstā́ Proto-Iranian *Hstā́bor.? Proto-Semitic *ʕaṯtar- Akkadian Ištarbor.? Old Persian 𐎠𐎿𐎫𐎼 (a-s-t-r)bor.

1000.t: From Biblical Hebrew טוֹבִיָּה (Ṭôḇiyyâ, literally “YHWH is my goodness”).
